newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov. says special session hinges on welfare.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov. says special session hinges on welfare.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki on Wednesday, confirming weeks of speculation, said that he only plans to recall the legislature for a special session if it appears likely that it will approve new welfare reforms.

While New York State in mid-October submitted an outline of its welfare program to Washington, in order to fully qualify for an estimated $2.4 billion block grant, the Republican governor has been working on a fuller plan.

New York, like most states, must revise its current system to comply with the new federal welfare program, which imposes stiff new limits, including work requirements and lifetime time limits, that became law in August.

The governor, who has said that the welfare reform, one of the most expensive and difficult issues facing the state, was complicating the budget process, on Wednesday said he had not yet decided whether he will submit a budget in December.

Saying he hoped to send the legislature detailed welfare proposals over the next few weeks, Pataki at a news conference in New York City said, "I'll only call them back if we have agreement or close to an agreement to achieve passage of welfare reform legislation."

The Democrat-led Assembly blocked the changes to the welfare system that Pataki had proposed in his 1997 fiscal budget, saying they were too harsh, and there are concerns the lower house again might reject some of the governor's plans.
However, Pataki might already have resolved at least some of the initial objections raised by the Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, according to sources in Albany.
Spokesmen for the Assembly and Senate were not immediately available to comment.

The governor, who led a bipartisan effort to win the voters' approval for a $1.75 billion bond act that will raise funds to clean up the state's air, water and land, said he hoped both parties would support the new welfare program.
Pataki, who said he expected informal negotiations between staff members instead of formal talks on welfare, was guarded about the prospects for success.
"I think there's a reasonable chance of getting it done. There's also a chance it won't get done, but we're going to try," he said.
